item.title: Anthropic promises to pursue humanity's benefit. Its IPO filing gives it wiggle room
item.description: When Anthropic goes public on Wall Street, the new pressure to deliver profits will test a commitment to prioritize humanity’s benefit as it develops AI.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: When Anthropic goes public on Wall Street, the new pressure to deliver profits will test a commitment it has made since its founding: to prioritize humanity’s benefit as it develops artificial intelligence. The San Francisco startup, which plans an initial public offering this month, has sketched out a governance structure that it says will protect the company’s broader mission against the pull of financial interests. But the mechanisms it describes give the company wide leeway to decide how to measure whether it’s benefiting society, experts say. Like its rival OpenAI, Anthropic is a public benefit corporation, a legal designation used by companies that pledge to balance shareholder interests with the public good. How that will play out for companies worth potentially trillions of dollars is uncharted territory. “I think then the real test emerges if and when the question of public benefit becomes costly” — or when the public benefit comes into conflict with making a profit, said Sarah Kreps, a professor and director of Cornell University’s Tech Policy Institute. In its regulatory filings, Anthropic pledges to pursue long-term benefits of humanity through the responsible development of advanced AI. “We strive to help bring humanity safely into an era where transformative AI exerts tremendous and potentially decisive influence over a broad range of human undertakings,” the company said. Anthropic also has pledged at least five per cent of its stock to a “public benefit” fund and its founders have committed to donate 80 per cent of their wealth. A pledge to do good is baked into corporate structure Other tech companies have pledged to do good including Google, which prominently featured its then-motto, “Don’t Be Evil,” in its investor prospectus when it went public in 2004. But the words were not legally binding, and critics have accused the tech giant of leaving them behind. Elon Musk’s takeover of Twitter in 2022 shows how the conflict between profit and public good might play out in real life, said Stavros Gadinis, a law professor at UC Berkeley School of Law. “Let’s say that Twitter’s directors felt that Elon was the wrong guy to police the public square because they didn’t trust him, they didn’t like him, they didn’t think he’d be fair, whatever it was,” Gadinis said. “But he made them an offer that was so high compared to what their advisors told them the company was really worth that it would be against their fiduciary duties to not sell to Elon. This is the situation that the public benefit charter is trying to avoid.” Had Twitter been a public benefit corporation, it could have been required to consider factors beyond maximizing shareholder value when selling the company. There aren’t many public benefit corporations whose shares are publicly traded and they are all much smaller than Anthropic and OpenAI. They include the eyewear company Warby Parker, the insurance company Lemonade and software developer Veeva Systems, which had a conventional corporate structure when it went public in 2013 and converted to a public benefit corporation in 2021. Anthropic’s idealistic ambitions for how it develops AI could run up against competitive pressure, such as from China, Kreps said. Anthropic and OpenAI’s models have gone from answering almost any question, even if it was dangerous, to becoming much more circumspect. But as they face more competition, including from open-source Chinese models that likely will tell you whatever you want, she said, “will they start to rethink some of those guardrails? And what happens then?” The setup generally is not preferred by shareholders because it gives more power to the company’s board than it does to shareholders. Whatever a company decides as its public benefit mission, it will likely be much more difficult to measure than profits. That’s particularly true for AI companies, whose leaders have exalted AI as the solution to many of humanity’s problems — from curing cancer to creating economic prosperity. “There are these echo chambers, the Silicon Valley bubble where they really think that what they’re doing is for the good of humanity,” Kreps said. And someone immersed in that environment, she added, might not even ask the right questions or understand how “public benefit” should be measured. A trust aims to hold Anthropic accountable A Long-Term Benefit Trust created by Anthropic is intended to operate as an independent body of trustees with expertise in AI safety, national security, public policy, and social enterprise. Through a special Class T common stock, the trust “generally has the authority to elect and remove” Class T directors, who together will constitute a majority of Anthropic’s board of directors, according to the IPO filing. The Class T common stock is a single share that allows the five trustees to vote as a unit. It has no economic rights — meaning they get to vote but they don’t see any financial benefit or losses from the share and can’t sell it. “The LTBT’s arrangements are designed to minimize the LTBT’s and the Trustees’ exposure to our financial performance and grant the Trustees sufficient independence to ensure we are striking this balance appropriately,” the filing said. Three of the company’s board directors are elected by the trust directly, and another three are elected by other shareholders, which include the company founders with a 50.1 per cent voting majority. A seventh director, with a potentially tie-breaking vote, is nominated by the trust and the holders of the Class T shares, but cannot be appointed or removed without consent from the board’s nominating committee, which is expected to be controlled by the founders. Effectively, the trust can only hold Anthropic accountable on issues such as AI safety and the company’s broader mission up to a point, Gadinis said. The trust “cannot determine the everyday decisions of these directors or the management of the company,” he said. ”If they disagree, they will have to go through the effort of removing directors, and they may not be able to remove a majority.” As a public company, Anthropic also will be required to report finances and generally be more transparent than a privately held one. Many public companies dealing with AI, including Google and Microsoft, regularly update the public on efforts to develop AI responsibly. The incentive for transparency could be as powerful as other mechanisms set up in Anthropic’s corporate structure, Gadinis said. “I do think that by being public, we are going to get a lot more information, because a lot of people are going to be asking questions, and companies will be responding to these questions. Not only because they’re required by security laws, but also because they want to build this kind of trust with the investing community,” he said. --- Barbara Ortutay, The Associated Press

item.title: Apple services hit by outage
item.description: Various Apple services were hit with outages on Tuesday, according to Apple’s system status site. Affected services include the App Store, Apple Music, and AppleCare on Device.
item.dc:creator: Kayla Thompson
item.content:encoded: Various Apple services were hit with outages on Tuesday, according to Apple’s system status site. The App Store and Apple Music were down briefly on Tuesday afternoon, but are now back online, according to the company. Outages remain on Schoolwork, Apple School Manager, and AppleCare on Device. An “issue” was identified on iCloud Account & Sign in. More details to come...

item.title: Higher jet fuel costs force Transat to explore options
item.description: Transat A.T. Inc. has hired financial advisers to help it evaluate potential financing and other opportunities as it deals with the impact of higher jet fuel prices.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: Firing off a warning signal about its cash flow, Transat A.T. Inc. has brought financial advisers on board as it struggles to staunch the losses caused by soaring jet fuel prices. The energy crisis triggered in February by war in the Middle East has meant Air Transat spends far more on fuel than it can recoup in ticket sales, given the leisure airline’s price-sensitive customers as well as its competition. The pricier jet kerosene added some $105 million in expenses in the three months ended Oct. 31 versus the same period a year earlier. That brings fuel costs from the war to nearly $280 million so far this year, a toll that amounts to nearly half of Transat’s fuel expense for all of last year. In a news release, the company called the oil crisis a “supply shock without historical precedent” and suggested it would leave a major dent in its earnings for the current quarter and the full fiscal year. “The corporation continues to manage its day-to-day business rigorously. However, its ability to pass higher fuel costs on to customers has remained so far limited which puts ongoing pressure on its financial position,” Transat said. “In this context, it has retained financial advisers to assist in evaluating all potential financing and other corporate opportunities and is seeking proposals in respect thereof.” The situation has already pushed Transat to seek emergency funding from Ottawa. The company secured $250 million in federal aid from the Canada Enterprise Emergency Funding Corp. in September. The low-interest line of credit came on top of a $150-million government loan in July. CEO Annick Guérard said earlier this fall that intense competition curtailed Transat’s ability to shift the swelling cost of fuel onto passengers’ shoulders. “There were big (capacity) increases on the Atlantic market,” she told analysts on a conference call in September. “When we introduced fuel surcharges, the demand went down. The whole Canadian market — competitors, everybody — started to launch promotions. And it never ended.” Those deals and discounts prevented Transat from raising ticket prices and forced it to tamp down some fees. “We’ve never seen such a highly competitive network,” Guérard said at the time. Observers say Transat should not be written off just yet, particularly in the light of Ottawa’s recent approach to foundering corporate ships in the sector. “We would caution against assuming that Transat’s financial challenges will necessarily translate into a meaningful reduction in competition, given the Canadian government’s historical willingness to support smaller airlines,” said analyst Savanthi Syth of Raymond James. She suggested a scale-down was more likely than a shutdown. “Ultimately, we view further Transat capacity rationalization — not an acquisition or exit — as the more plausible source of upside for Air Canada, although the magnitude and timing remain uncertain,” she said in a note to investors. As for the possibility of a merger, “history suggests significant hurdles,” Syth added. Air Canada had been on track to buy the company after reaching a deal in 2019, but COVID-19 and then European red tape tripped up that plan. An earlier $720-million purchase price was watered down to $190 million in October 2020 as the pandemic devastated the airline industry. The federal government greenlit the transaction in early 2021, but the European Commission raised competition concerns over transatlantic routes, prompting the parties to call off the agreement. -- This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

item.title: Martin Cobb’s Top Picks for Nov. 17, 2026
item.description: As judged by the S&P 500 index level, the U.S. market was down in October. But the average stock therein was up. Indeed, the S&P 500 equal weighted index returned almost five per cent over the month, ...
item.content:encoded:
Martin Cobb, Senior Vice-President, Equities, Lorne Steinberg Wealth Management Focus: U.S. & Canadian Equities

Top Picks: WSP Global , PepsiCo , Alphabet MARKET OUTLOOK: Demand and supply. In any marketplace, price is set by the interaction of these two forces. A stock market is no different. Putting aside the competition from higher yielding bonds today, there has been a marked shift within the equity market itself. The third quarter saw yet another quite remarkable growth in earnings per share for the S&P 500, with something in the region of 30 per cent underlying progression versus the same period 12 months ago. But, despite that, the free cash flow generated from these same entities actually contracted year over year. For the better part of a decade, the stock market has been, in effect, a cannibal, using massive free cash flow to shrink the supply of public equity. Today, that equation is flipping in real time. Not only are we witnessing record initial public offerings (IPOs) but the very companies that were once reliable buyers of their own shares and now issuing them in size. While a US$75 trillion market can undoubtedly absorb this, the several hundred billion dollars in fresh supply compares with typically less than US$50 billion in any one year. What was once a reliable tailwind has shifted into a notable headwind. As judged by the S&P 500 index level, the U.S. market was down in October. But the average stock therein was up. Indeed, the S&P 500 equal weighted index returned almost five per cent over the month, the widest margin of monthly outperformance versus its market cap weighted peer since 2009. November is proving similar. How to set BNN Bloomberg as your preferred source on Google Market-moving news, fast:  Get the BNN Bloomberg App now Sign up for the Market Call Top Picks newsletter at  bnnbloomberg.ca/newsletters TOP PICKS: Martin Cobb’s Top Picks: WSP Global, PepsiCo & Alphabet Martin Cobb, senior vice-president in equities at Lorne Steinberg Wealth Management, iA Private Wealth, shares his top stock picks to watch in the market.

WSP Global (WSP TSX) A Canada to the world success story that today is a leading global professional services firm providing engineering, design, and strategic advisory services. Operate as a pure play consulting entity (i.e. take no construction risk) across a variety of sectors (such as transportation, infrastructure, property, utilities etc.) and with a particular strength in power & energy. Grown significantly through merge and acquisitions (M&A), with mid-teens average annual sales growth and profits compounding at an even higher rate Supposedly artificial intelligence (AI) is going to do away with the need for all sorts of consulting or certification businesses, including those that are, by nature, very manual in their process As a result, the stock’s valuation has collapsed: having historically commanded a mid 20s forward earning multiple during this past decade, today it sits on about 14 times 2027 And with the prospect of continued double-digit eps growt PepsiCo (PEP NASDAQ) Now more of a foods / snacks business than it is beverages Drinks brands include the eponymous one, Gatorade, Mountain Dew, Lipton, and various waters (incl Bubly) The food side’s key brands are Lays, Doritos and Cheetos Unlike Coca-Cola (which sells syrup) PepsiCo is fully vertically integrated and indeed views the ability to distribute to the same customer as a key competitive advantage Not a huge top line grower: maybe two to three per cent organic growth (but reasonably consistent) With a little bit of ongoing margin accretion, combined with ongoing portfolio activity, eps growth should at least reach mid single digits Pays out most of FCF in dividends (yield today just over four per cent) and has grown its payout consistently for 54 years now, i.e. a true dividend aristocrat Nothing really has changed in recent years other than a sustained compression in the multiple investors have been willing to pay (historically 20 times plus was the norm) Now commanding a 17 times forward earnings multiple: that seems on the low side (Coke is on 28 times just for comparison Alphabet (GOOGL NASDAQ) Best known as the parent of Google, Alphabet is an advertising juggernaut with strong positions in search (Google), video (YouTube), and mobile (Android), with 90 per cent plus share in global online search Core advertising business still growing solidly despite admittedly facing challenges Firmly the third player globally in cloud behind AWS and Azure, but growing faster and with a strong upwards drive in profitability (Google Cloud’s margins are close to half of that of the other two) YouTube (which they paid less than $2 billion for in 2006) now has revenues above those of Netflix Massive optionality in “Other Bets” including driverless cars (Waymo), quantum computing, medical tech, AR/VR, machine learning etc. Large language models pose possibly the first ever real threat to Google’s search business. But must be put into context: perhaps 20 per cent of group revenues is at risk and Alphabet is not exactly sitting idle Over $100 billion in net cash and generating about twice that today in annual operating cashflow Admittedly spending a lot and decided on an opportunistic capital raising (not terribly enthused by that but at least it was at a share price north of $350) Share price has retraced markedly in recent months, with the stock trading at or below 20 times and 16 times anticipated earnings for 2027 and 2028 respectively DISCLOSURE PERSONAL FAMILY PORTFOLIO/FUND WSP TSX Y Y Y PEP NASD Y Y Y GOOGL NASD Y Y Y PAST PICKS: NOV. 26, 2025 Martin Cobb’s Past Picks: Kenvue, Starbucks & Canadian National Railway Martin Cobb, senior vice-president in equities at Lorne Steinberg Wealth Management, iA Private Wealth, discusses his past stock picks and how they’re doing.
